title: Injection Attacks: A Field Handbook
summary: How untrusted input becomes executed code across SQL, HTML/JS, and OS shells, and the two defenses that actually work: parameterisation and context-aware output encoding.

chapters.title: What Injection Is
points: Definition: attacker-supplied data crosses a boundary and gets interpreted as code/commands instead of inert data
Root cause: mixing untrusted data with a control string (query, markup, shell command) using string concatenation
The confusion: an interpreter cannot tell where developer intent ends and attacker input begins when both arrive as one flat string
Trust boundary: any point where data from an untrusted source (HTTP params, headers, cookies, uploaded files, upstream services) enters an interpreter
Interpreter examples: SQL engine, HTML/JS parser in browser, OS shell (/bin/sh, cmd.exe), LDAP, XPath, NoSQL, template engines
Impact spectrum: data theft, auth bypass, data tampering, remote code execution, full host compromise, lateral movement
Injection sits at/near the top of OWASP Top 10 for over a decade; A03:2021 folds XSS into Injection
Core insight for the whole handbook: the fix is structural separation of code from data, not filtering 'bad characters'

chapters.title: SQL Injection — Mechanics
points: Vulnerable pattern: "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name='" + input + "'" concatenates input into query text
Classic auth bypass payload: ' OR '1'='1 makes the WHERE clause always true
Comment truncation: input like admin'-- cuts off the rest of the query (password check) using -- or #
UNION-based extraction: ' UNION SELECT username,password FROM users-- pulls data from other tables (needs matching column count/types)
Stacked queries: '; DROP TABLE users-- runs a second statement where the driver allows multiple statements
Blind boolean SQLi: no data returned, but page differs on true vs false (AND 1=1 vs AND 1=2) to infer data bit by bit
Blind time-based SQLi: inject SLEEP(5)/pg_sleep(5)/WAITFOR DELAY to read data via response latency when there is zero visible feedback
Error-based SQLi: force DB error messages that leak column names, versions, and data
Second-order SQLi: payload stored safely, then later concatenated into a query on a different code path
Reconnaissance: version() / @@version, information_schema.tables/columns to map the database

chapters.title: Parameterised Queries — The Real Fix
points: Prepared statement: query template with placeholders (? or :name) sent to DB separately from the values
Why it works: the SQL structure is parsed and compiled before values bind, so a value can never become new syntax
Bound values are always treated as literal data — ' OR '1'='1 becomes a literal string searched for, not logic
Placeholder styles: positional (?) vs named (:id, @id, $1) depending on driver
Example (Python): cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name=%s", (name,)) — never % string formatting
Example (Java): PreparedStatement with setString(1, name)
Limitation: placeholders bind values only, NOT identifiers (table/column names) or keywords like ASC/DESC
Dynamic identifiers must use a strict allowlist mapping user choice to a fixed set of known-safe names
ORMs (Hibernate, SQLAlchemy, ActiveRecord) parameterise by default — but raw()/text()/string interpolation reopens the hole
Stored procedures help only if they themselves parameterise; dynamic SQL inside a proc is still vulnerable
Least privilege as defense-in-depth: app DB account should not own DROP/DDL or read other schemas

chapters.title: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
points: Definition: attacker JavaScript executes in a victim's browser in the trusted origin of the vulnerable site
Reflected XSS: payload in the request (URL/param) echoed straight into the response, delivered via a crafted link
Stored/persistent XSS: payload saved server-side (comment, profile, message) and served to every viewer — highest blast radius
DOM-based XSS: vulnerability is client-side; JS writes untrusted data (location.hash) into a sink like innerHTML with no server round-trip
Dangerous sinks: innerHTML, outerHTML, document.write, eval, setTimeout(string), element.setAttribute('href', ...) for javascript: URIs
Impact: session cookie theft (document.cookie), session riding, keylogging, credential phishing, CSRF token theft, worm propagation
Sources of untrusted data in the DOM: location, document.referrer, window.name, postMessage, and stored server data
Mutation XSS (mXSS): browser re-parses/normalises HTML so a sanitised-looking string becomes executable after insertion
HttpOnly cookies blunt cookie theft but not other XSS actions (making requests as the user, defacement, keylogging)

chapters.title: Output Encoding & Preventing XSS
points: Core rule: encode untrusted data at output time, for the exact context it lands in — encoding is context-specific
HTML body context: encode < > & " ' to < > & " ' so text can't open tags
HTML attribute context: quote the attribute and entity-encode; unquoted attributes are exploitable with spaces/event handlers
JavaScript context: use JS string escaping or, better, inject data as JSON via a data-* attribute and read it, never build script from strings
URL context: percent-encode (encodeURIComponent) and validate the scheme — block javascript:/data: in href/src
CSS context: encode within style values; untrusted CSS enables data exfiltration and expression()-style abuse
Prefer safe sinks: textContent/innerText over innerHTML; createElement + setAttribute over building HTML strings
Framework auto-escaping (React JSX, Angular, Vue, Django/Jinja templates) encodes by default — the danger is the escape hatch (dangerouslySetInnerHTML, v-html, |safe, bypassSecurityTrust)
When you must accept HTML: sanitise with a vetted allowlist library (DOMPurify), never a hand-rolled regex blocklist
Content-Security-Policy (CSP) as defense-in-depth: restrict script sources, block inline script; not a substitute for encoding
Encode on output, not input: the same data may be rendered into multiple contexts, each needing different encoding

chapters.title: Command Injection
points: Definition: untrusted input reaches an OS shell command, letting attacker run arbitrary system commands
Vulnerable pattern: os.system("ping " + host) / exec("convert " + filename) via a shell
Shell metacharacters that chain commands: ; | & && || $(...) `...` newline > <
Example payload: host = "8.8.8.8; cat /etc/passwd" runs the second command as the app user
Argument injection: even without a shell, leading - lets input pose as a flag (e.g. a filename starting with --) changing program behavior
The fix: don't invoke a shell — use array/exec APIs that pass args directly to the process (execve, subprocess with a list, no shell=True)
Python: subprocess.run(['ping','-c','1', host]) with shell=False — never shell=True with concatenation
Node: execFile/spawn with an args array instead of exec(cmd_string)
If a shell is unavoidable: strict allowlist of permitted values and proper quoting/escaping (shlex.quote) — blocklists leak
Prefer native language libraries over shelling out (HTTP client vs curl, file APIs vs cp) to remove the interpreter entirely
Run with least privilege and in a sandbox/container so a breakout is contained

chapters.title: Input Validation vs Encoding vs Parameterisation
points: Three distinct controls, often confused: validation (is this data acceptable?), parameterisation (separate code from data at the DB), encoding (make data safe for one output context)
Validation is defense-in-depth, NOT a primary injection defense — valid data can still be a valid attack (O'Brien is a legitimate name and a SQL breaker)
Allowlist (accept only known-good: pattern, type, range, set) beats blocklist (reject known-bad), which always misses encodings/variants
Canonicalisation first: decode to one form before validating, or attackers slip past with %3C, double-encoding, unicode homoglyphs, overlong UTF-8
Parameterisation is the primary fix for SQL; array-exec is the primary fix for commands; context encoding is the primary fix for XSS
Right layer matters: escaping for SQL does not make data safe for HTML, and vice versa — no universal 'sanitise' function
Type coercion as a free defense: casting an id to int makes SQLi in that field structurally impossible
Combine layers: validate at entry, parameterise/encode at each interpreter boundary, least privilege underneath

chapters.title: Common Mistakes & Anti-Patterns
points: Blocklist filtering (stripping quotes/keywords): bypassed via case, comments (SEL/**/ECT), encoding, and whitespace tricks
Escaping quotes by hand: misses numeric contexts (no quotes needed), backslash edge cases, and charset-based bypasses
'Sanitise once on input' then reuse everywhere: wrong context on output re-introduces the flaw
Trusting client-side validation: attacker sends raw requests bypassing the browser entirely
Parameterising values but concatenating table/column/ORDER BY from user input — the classic remaining hole
Using shell=True / exec(string) 'because the args are internal' — internal today, user-influenced tomorrow (second-order)
Assuming an ORM is automatically safe while using raw query escape hatches
Disabling framework auto-escaping (dangerouslySetInnerHTML, |safe) for convenience without sanitising
Relying on WAF as the fix rather than a stopgap — WAFs are bypassable and buy time, not safety
Verbose DB/stack error messages in production that hand attackers schema and version details

chapters.title: Summary & Defense Checklist
points: One mental model: every injection is code/data confusion at an interpreter boundary — keep them separate
SQL: always parameterise; allowlist identifiers; least-privilege DB account; never concatenate
XSS: context-aware output encoding; safe sinks (textContent); sanitise HTML with DOMPurify; CSP + HttpOnly as depth
Command: avoid the shell, pass args as an array; allowlist + sandbox + least privilege when a shell is unavoidable
Validation is a supporting layer (allowlist, canonicalise first), never the sole defense
Encode/parameterise at output/boundary time and per-context, not once at input
Defense in depth: layer validation, parameterisation, encoding, least privilege, and CSP so one failure isn't fatal
Verify continuously: code review of query/exec/render sinks, SAST/DAST, and dependency updates for the interpreters and libraries you rely on
